questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
Whether we feel happy or sad, content or discontent, [ is not determined / are not determined ] merely by each individual successive moment of life experience — a good thing happens and I’m happy, a bad thing happens and I’m sad.
questions.e: Whether we feel ... 전체가 하나의 명사절 주어이므로 단수 동사 is를 쓴다. 감정이 경험에 의해 결정되는 관계이므로 수동태이다.

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
While our experiences affect our mood, we are not [ blew / blown ] in a completely new direction by each gust of wind.
questions.e: be동사 뒤에서 수동태를 이루므로 blow의 과거분사 blown을 쓴다. blew는 과거형이다.

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
As humans, we adjust — to new information and events both good and bad — and [ return / returning ] to our personal default level of well-being.
questions.e: 주어 we에 대해 adjust와 return이 and로 연결된 병렬 동사이다. 중간의 대시는 부연 표현이므로 문장의 뼈대를 끊지 않는다.

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
There will be highs and lows, but over time, like water [ sought / seeking ] its own level, we are pulled toward our baseline — back up after bad news and back down after good.
questions.e: 물이 자기 수위를 찾는 능동 관계이므로 seeking을 쓴다. like water ...는 기준선 복귀를 설명하는 비유이다.

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
The euphoria of first love fades, and so [ does / is ] the despair of a break-up.
questions.e: 앞의 fades는 일반동사이고 뒤의 주어 despair가 단수이므로 so does the despair ...가 된다. does는 fades를 대신한다.

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
This tendency is best seen with little kids and their toy joy: When they get [ that / what ] they’ve longed for, they believe they will be happy for the rest of their lives.
questions.e: what they’ve longed for는 ‘그들이 간절히 원해 온 것’이라는 뜻이며 get의 목적어이다. for의 목적어 자리도 what이 담당한다.

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
And for the first few minutes of the rest of their lives, they [ are / do ].
questions.e: they are 뒤에는 앞 문장의 happy가 생략되어 있다. be happy의 구조를 이어받으므로 do로 바꿀 수 없다.

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
But then the kids — like adults — [ adapts / adapt ].
questions.e: 주어 the kids는 복수이므로 adapt를 쓴다. like adults는 삽입된 비교 표현이다.

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
Whether we feel happy or sad, content or discontent, is not determined [ entirely independently / merely ] by each individual successive moment of life experience — a good thing happens and I’m happy, a bad thing happens and I’m sad.
questions.e: 경험이 영향을 주지 않는다는 뜻이 아니라 매 순간의 경험만으로 감정이 결정되지는 않는다는 뜻이다.

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
While our experiences affect our mood, we are [ not blown / permanently carried away ] in a completely new direction by each gust of wind.
questions.e: 기분이 변해도 매번 완전히 새로운 행복 수준으로 옮겨 가는 것은 아니다.

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
As humans, we adjust — to new information and events both good and bad — and return to our personal [ constantly rising peak / default level ] of well-being.
questions.e: 경험에 적응한 뒤 돌아가는 개인의 기준 수준이 핵심 개념이다.

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
There will be highs and lows, but over time, like water seeking its own level, we are pulled toward our [ baseline / endless extreme ] — back up after bad news and back down after good.
questions.e: 좋고 나쁜 경험 이후 모두 개인의 기준선으로 되돌아간다는 비유이다.

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
The euphoria of first love [ lasts forever / fades ], and so does the despair of a break-up.
questions.e: 행복과 절망의 강도 모두 시간이 지나며 약해진다는 예시이다.

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
This tendency is best seen with little kids and their toy joy: When they get what they’ve longed for, they believe they will be happy [ for the rest of their lives / only for a second ].
c: for the rest of their lives
questions.a: for the rest of their lives
questions.e: 아이는 새 장난감의 기쁨이 평생 이어질 것이라고 믿지만 다음 문장에서 그 기대가 뒤집힌다.

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
And for the [ entire lifetime / first few minutes ] of the rest of their lives, they are.
questions.e: 아이가 예상한 평생의 행복은 실제로는 처음 몇 분에 한정된다.

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
But then the kids — like adults — [ adapt / remain unchanged ].
questions.e: 새로운 장난감의 기쁨에도 적응해 기본 수준으로 돌아간다는 결론이다.

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 다음 문장의 “merely”은(는) ‘단지’(으)로 해석된다.
Whether we feel happy or sad, content or discontent, is not determined merely by each individual successive moment of life experience — a good thing happens and I’m happy, a bad thing happens and I’m sad.
questions.e: merely = 단지

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 다음 문장의 “not blown”은(는) ‘알지 못한 채’(으)로 해석된다.
While our experiences affect our mood, we are not blown in a completely new direction by each gust of wind.
questions.e: not blown = 날아가지 않는다

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 다음 문장의 “default level”은(는) ‘기본 행복 수준’(으)로 해석된다.
As humans, we adjust — to new information and events both good and bad — and return to our personal default level of well-being.
questions.e: default level = 기본 행복 수준

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 다음 문장의 “baseline”은(는) ‘기준선’(으)로 해석된다.
There will be highs and lows, but over time, like water seeking its own level, we are pulled toward our baseline — back up after bad news and back down after good.
questions.e: baseline = 기준선

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 다음 문장의 “fades”은(는) ‘사라지고’(으)로 해석된다.
The euphoria of first love fades, and so does the despair of a break-up.
questions.e: fades = 사라지고

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 다음 문장의 “for the rest of their lives”은(는) ‘추적하고’(으)로 해석된다.
This tendency is best seen with little kids and their toy joy: When they get what they’ve longed for, they believe they will be happy for the rest of their lives.
questions.e: for the rest of their lives = 남은 인생 동안

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 다음 문장의 “first few minutes”은(는) ‘역시’(으)로 해석된다.
And for the first few minutes of the rest of their lives, they are.
questions.e: first few minutes = 처음 몇 분 동안

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 다음 문장의 “adapt”은(는) ‘부분적인 반영’(으)로 해석된다.
But then the kids — like adults — adapt.
questions.e: adapt = 적응한다

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 순서로 알맞은 것은?
Whether we feel happy or sad, content or discontent, is not determined merely by each individual successive moment of life experience — a good thing happens and I’m happy, a bad thing happens and I’m sad.

(A) This tendency is best seen with little kids and their toy joy: When they get what they’ve longed for, they believe they will be happy for the rest of their lives. And for the first few minutes of the rest of their lives, they are. But then the kids — like adults — adapt.
(B) While our experiences affect our mood, we are not blown in a completely new direction by each gust of wind. As humans, we adjust — to new information and events both good and bad — and return to our personal default level of well-being.
(C) There will be highs and lows, but over time, like water seeking its own level, we are pulled toward our baseline — back up after bad news and back down after good. The euphoria of first love fades, and so does the despair of a break-up.
questions.e: 감정은 매 순간의 좋은 일과 나쁜 일만으로 결정되지 않는다. → 사람은 경험에 적응하고 기본 행복 수준으로 돌아간다. → 제 수위를 찾는 물처럼 첫사랑과 이별의 감정도 약해진다. → 장난감을 얻은 아이도 잠시 행복한 뒤 적응한다.

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 우리말에 맞게 낱말을 모두 배열해 영어 문장을 쓰세요.
첫사랑의 행복감은 사라지고 결별의 절망도 그렇다.

fades, / of / first / so / love / of / The / the / euphoria / despair / a / break-up / does / and
questions.a: The euphoria of first love fades, and so does the despair of a break-up
questions.e: 첫사랑의 행복감은 사라지고 결별의 절망도 그렇다.

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 우리말에 맞게 낱말을 모두 배열해 영어 문장을 쓰세요.
그리고 그들의 남은 인생의 처음 몇 분 동안 그들은 그렇다.

And / the / they / first / rest / of / for / are / minutes / of / lives, / their / few / the
questions.a: And for the first few minutes of the rest of their lives, they are
questions.e: 그리고 그들의 남은 인생의 처음 몇 분 동안 그들은 그렇다.

questions.q:
[11-12 기쁨도 슬픔도 결국 제자리로] 우리말에 맞게 낱말을 모두 배열해 영어 문장을 쓰세요.
하지만 그다음에 아이들은 어른들처럼 적응한다.

like / But / kids / the / adapt / — / — / then / adults
questions.a: But then the kids — like adults — adapt
questions.e: 하지만 그다음에 아이들은 어른들처럼 적응한다.

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
Although you may put off [ going / to go ] to sleep in order to squeeze more activities into your day, eventually your need for sleep becomes overwhelming and you are forced to get some sleep.
questions.e: put off는 ‘미루다’라는 뜻으로 뒤에 동명사 going이 온다. in order to squeeze는 활동을 더 넣으려는 목적을 나타낸다.

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
This daily drive for sleep appears to be due, in part, to a compound [ knowing / known ] as adenosine.
questions.e: compound는 아데노신이라는 이름으로 알려진 대상이므로 known을 쓴다. known as는 ‘~로 알려진’이라는 뜻이다.

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
This natural chemical builds up in your blood as time awake [ increases / increase ].
questions.e: as절의 주어는 단수명사 time이고 awake는 깨어 있는 상태를 덧붙이므로 동사는 increases이다.

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
While you sleep, your body [ break / breaks ] down the adenosine.
questions.e: 주절 주어 your body는 단수이므로 breaks를 쓴다. while절의 you를 주절 주어로 착각하지 않는다.

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
Thus, this molecule may be what your body uses to keep track of lost sleep and to trigger sleep when [ needed / needing ].
questions.e: when needed는 when sleep is needed의 생략 표현이다. 수면이 필요한 대상이므로 과거분사 needed를 쓴다.

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
An accumulation of adenosine and other factors might explain why, after several nights of less than optimal amounts of sleep, you build up a sleep debt that you must make up by [ sleep / sleeping ] longer than normal.
questions.e: by sleeping longer는 ‘더 오래 잠으로써’라는 수단이다. 전치사 by 뒤에 동명사를 쓴다.

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
Because of such built-in molecular feedback, you can’t become accustomed to [ getting / get ] less sleep than your body needs.
questions.e: become accustomed to에서 to는 전치사이므로 동명사 getting이 온다. ‘~에 익숙해지다’라는 표현이다.

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
Eventually, a lack of sleep [ catch / catches ] up with you.
questions.e: 주어의 핵심은 단수 lack이다. of sleep은 수식어이므로 catches를 쓴다. catch up with는 결국 영향을 미친다는 뜻이다.

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
Although you may put off going to sleep in order to squeeze more activities into your day, eventually your need for sleep becomes [ negligible / overwhelming ] and you are forced to get some sleep.
questions.e: 수면을 미루어도 결국 수면 욕구가 감당하기 어려울 만큼 커진다.

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
This daily drive for sleep appears to be due, in part, to a compound known as [ adenosine / oxygen ].
questions.e: 본문은 수면 욕구와 관련된 물질로 아데노신을 제시한다.

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
This natural chemical [ breaks down / builds up ] in your blood as time awake increases.
questions.e: 깨어 있는 시간이 늘어날수록 아데노신은 축적된다.

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
While you sleep, your body [ breaks down / accumulates ] the adenosine.
questions.e: 깨어 있을 때의 축적과 반대로, 수면 중에는 아데노신이 분해된다.

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
Thus, this molecule may be what your body uses to [ erase all records of / keep track of ] lost sleep and to trigger sleep when needed.
questions.e: 아데노신은 놓친 수면을 기록하고 필요할 때 잠을 유도하는 피드백 물질로 설명된다.

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
An accumulation of adenosine and other factors might explain why, after several nights of less than optimal amounts of sleep, you build up a [ sleep debt / permanent immunity ] that you must make up by sleeping longer than normal.
questions.e: 부족한 잠은 사라지지 않고 나중에 더 자서 보충해야 할 빚처럼 쌓인다.

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
Because of such built-in molecular feedback, you [ can easily / can’t ] become accustomed to getting less sleep than your body needs.
questions.e: 몸의 피드백 때문에 필요한 양보다 적은 수면에 적응할 수 없다는 핵심 결론이다.

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
Eventually, a lack of sleep [ catches up with / disappears from ] you.
questions.e: 수면 부족은 결국 몸에 영향을 미치며 회피할 수 없다는 마무리이다.

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 다음 문장의 “overwhelming”은(는) ‘압도적이게’(으)로 해석된다.
Although you may put off going to sleep in order to squeeze more activities into your day, eventually your need for sleep becomes overwhelming and you are forced to get some sleep.
questions.e: overwhelming = 압도적이게

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 다음 문장의 “adenosine”은(는) ‘아데노신’(으)로 해석된다.
This daily drive for sleep appears to be due, in part, to a compound known as adenosine.
questions.e: adenosine = 아데노신

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 다음 문장의 “builds up”은(는) ‘쌓인다’(으)로 해석된다.
This natural chemical builds up in your blood as time awake increases.
questions.e: builds up = 쌓인다

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 다음 문장의 “breaks down”은(는) ‘분해한다’(으)로 해석된다.
While you sleep, your body breaks down the adenosine.
questions.e: breaks down = 분해한다

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 다음 문장의 “keep track of”은(는) ‘들을 수 없는’(으)로 해석된다.
Thus, this molecule may be what your body uses to keep track of lost sleep and to trigger sleep when needed.
questions.e: keep track of = 추적하고

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 다음 문장의 “sleep debt”은(는) ‘특정한 색상, 모양, 혹은 크기를 갖고 있지 않다’(으)로 해석된다.
An accumulation of adenosine and other factors might explain why, after several nights of less than optimal amounts of sleep, you build up a sleep debt that you must make up by sleeping longer than normal.
questions.e: sleep debt = 수면 빚

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 다음 문장의 “can’t”은(는) ‘정신적으로’(으)로 해석된다.
Because of such built-in molecular feedback, you can’t become accustomed to getting less sleep than your body needs.
questions.e: can’t = 익숙해질 수 없다

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 다음 문장의 “catches up with”은(는) ‘따라잡는다’(으)로 해석된다.
Eventually, a lack of sleep catches up with you.
questions.e: catches up with = 따라잡는다

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 순서로 알맞은 것은?
Although you may put off going to sleep in order to squeeze more activities into your day, eventually your need for sleep becomes overwhelming and you are forced to get some sleep.

(A) An accumulation of adenosine and other factors might explain why, after several nights of less than optimal amounts of sleep, you build up a sleep debt that you must make up by sleeping longer than normal. Because of such built-in molecular feedback, you can’t become accustomed to getting less sleep than your body needs. Eventually, a lack of sleep catches up with you.
(B) This daily drive for sleep appears to be due, in part, to a compound known as adenosine. This natural chemical builds up in your blood as time awake increases.
(C) While you sleep, your body breaks down the adenosine. Thus, this molecule may be what your body uses to keep track of lost sleep and to trigger sleep when needed.
questions.e: 잠을 미뤄도 결국 수면 욕구가 압도한다. → 아데노신은 깨어 있으면 쌓이고 자는 동안 분해된다. → 잃은 잠을 추적하는 피드백으로 수면 빚을 보충하게 된다. → 필요한 양보다 적은 수면에 익숙해질 수 없고 부족은 결국 따라잡는다.

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 우리말에 맞게 낱말을 모두 배열해 영어 문장을 쓰세요.
이 자연 화학물질은 깨어 있는 시간이 증가할수록 당신의 혈액 속에 쌓인다.

blood / in / time / your / as / builds / natural / This / up / awake / increases / chemical
questions.a: This natural chemical builds up in your blood as time awake increases
questions.e: 이 자연 화학물질은 깨어 있는 시간이 증가할수록 당신의 혈액 속에 쌓인다.

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 우리말에 맞게 낱말을 모두 배열해 영어 문장을 쓰세요.
당신이 자는 동안 당신의 몸은 아데노신을 분해한다.

the / While / your / body / you / adenosine / breaks / sleep, / down
questions.a: While you sleep, your body breaks down the adenosine
questions.e: 당신이 자는 동안 당신의 몸은 아데노신을 분해한다.

questions.q:
[11-13 수면 부족은 결국 따라잡는다] 우리말에 맞게 낱말을 모두 배열해 영어 문장을 쓰세요.
결국 수면 부족은 당신을 따라잡는다.

a / up / lack / you / Eventually, / of / sleep / with / catches
questions.a: Eventually, a lack of sleep catches up with you
questions.e: 결국 수면 부족은 당신을 따라잡는다.

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
One of the things that makes uncertainty difficult for members of the public [ to appreciate / appreciating ] is that the significance of uncertainty is relative.
questions.e: difficult for members of the public to appreciate에서 for 이하는 to부정사의 의미상 주어를 나타낸다. uncertainty는 appreciate의 의미상 목적어이다.

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
Take, for example, the distance between Earth and the sun: 1.49597 × 10⁸ km, as [ measuring / measured ] at one point during the year.
questions.e: 거리는 측정하는 주체가 아니라 측정된 대상이므로 measured를 쓴다. as measured는 as it is measured의 생략으로 이해할 수 있다.

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
This seems relatively precise; after all, using six significant digits [ means / mean ] I know the distance to an accuracy of one part in a million or so.
questions.e: using six significant digits 전체가 주어인 동명사구이므로 단수 동사 means를 쓴다. digits가 복수라고 mean을 쓰지 않는다.

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
However, if the next digit is uncertain, that means the uncertainty in knowing the precise Earth–sun distance is [ largest / larger ] than the distance between New York and Chicago!
questions.e: 두 거리의 크기를 비교하므로 larger than을 쓴다. largest는 최상급이므로 이 비교 구조에 맞지 않는다.

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
Whether or not the quoted number is “precise” therefore [ depends / depend ] on what I’m intending to do with it.
questions.e: whether절 전체가 하나의 주어이므로 단수 동사 depends를 쓴다. what절은 전치사 on의 목적어이다.

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
If I care only about what minute the sun will rise tomorrow, then the number [ quoting / quoted ] here is fine.
questions.e: number는 인용된 대상이므로 quoted가 뒤에서 수식한다. quoting은 숫자가 무언가를 인용하는 능동 의미가 되어 문맥에 맞지 않는다.

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
If I want to send a satellite to orbit just above the sun, however, then I would need to know distances more [ accurately / accurate ].
questions.e: 거리를 아는 정확한 방식을 나타내어 know를 수식하므로 부사 accurately를 쓴다. more accurately는 더 정확하게라는 비교 표현이다.

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
One of the things that makes uncertainty difficult for members of the public to appreciate is that the significance of uncertainty is [ absolute / relative ].
questions.e: 불확실성이 얼마나 중요한지는 목적과 맥락에 따라 달라진다는 주장이다.

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
Take, for example, the distance between Earth and the sun: [ 1.49597 × 10⁸ / 1.49597 × 10⁴ ] km, as measured at one point during the year.
questions.e: 원문은 지구와 태양의 거리를 큰 수로 제시하여 상대적 정밀도와 실제 오차 크기를 대비한다.

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
This seems [ perfectly exact / relatively precise ]; after all, using six significant digits means I know the distance to an accuracy of one part in a million or so.
questions.e: 수치가 상대적으로 정밀해 보여도 모든 목적에 오차가 무시할 만한 것은 아니라는 전개이다.

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
However, if the next digit is [ uncertain / perfectly certain ], that means the uncertainty in knowing the precise Earth–sun distance is larger than the distance between New York and Chicago!
questions.e: 다음 자리의 불확실성이 실제 거리로는 클 수 있다는 원문의 대비이다.

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
Whether or not the quoted number is “precise” therefore depends on [ how impressive it looks / what I’m intending to do ] with it.
questions.e: 숫자가 충분히 정밀한지는 그 숫자를 어떤 목적에 쓸지에 달려 있다.

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
If I care only about what minute the sun will rise tomorrow, then the number quoted here is [ fine / entirely useless ].
questions.e: 일출 시각을 분 단위로 알고 싶은 목적에는 제시한 수치로 충분하다는 예시이다.

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
If I want to send a satellite to orbit just above the sun, however, then I would need to know distances [ less accurately / more accurately ].
questions.e: 위성 궤도 계산에는 일출 시각을 대략 아는 것보다 더 높은 정확도가 필요하다.

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 다음 문장의 “relative”은(는) ‘더 정확하게’(으)로 해석된다.
One of the things that makes uncertainty difficult for members of the public to appreciate is that the significance of uncertainty is relative.
questions.e: relative = 상대적

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 다음 문장의 “1.49597 × 10⁸”은(는) ‘처음 몇 분 동안’(으)로 해석된다.
Take, for example, the distance between Earth and the sun: 1.49597 × 10⁸ km, as measured at one point during the year.

[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 다음 문장의 “relatively precise”은(는) ‘상대적으로 정확해’(으)로 해석된다.
This seems relatively precise; after all, using six significant digits means I know the distance to an accuracy of one part in a million or so.
questions.e: relatively precise = 상대적으로 정확해

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 다음 문장의 “uncertain”은(는) ‘불확실하다면’(으)로 해석된다.
However, if the next digit is uncertain, that means the uncertainty in knowing the precise Earth–sun distance is larger than the distance between New York and Chicago!
questions.e: uncertain = 불확실하다면

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 다음 문장의 “what I’m intending to do”은(는) ‘무엇을 하려고 하느냐’(으)로 해석된다.
Whether or not the quoted number is “precise” therefore depends on what I’m intending to do with it.
questions.e: what I’m intending to do = 무엇을 하려고 하느냐

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 다음 문장의 “fine”은(는) ‘관찰 결과’(으)로 해석된다.
If I care only about what minute the sun will rise tomorrow, then the number quoted here is fine.
questions.e: fine = 괜찮다

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 다음 문장의 “more accurately”은(는) ‘녹음’(으)로 해석된다.
If I want to send a satellite to orbit just above the sun, however, then I would need to know distances more accurately.
questions.e: more accurately = 더 정확하게

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 순서로 알맞은 것은?
One of the things that makes uncertainty difficult for members of the public to appreciate is that the significance of uncertainty is relative.

(A) If I care only about what minute the sun will rise tomorrow, then the number quoted here is fine. If I want to send a satellite to orbit just above the sun, however, then I would need to know distances more accurately.
(B) Take, for example, the distance between Earth and the sun: 1.49597 × 10⁸ km, as measured at one point during the year. This seems relatively precise; after all, using six significant digits means I know the distance to an accuracy of one part in a million or so.
(C) However, if the next digit is uncertain, that means the uncertainty in knowing the precise Earth–sun distance is larger than the distance between New York and Chicago! Whether or not the quoted number is “precise” therefore depends on what I’m intending to do with it.
questions.e: 불확실성의 중요성은 상대적이다. → 지구와 태양 사이 거리를 여섯 자리 유효 숫자로 제시한다. → 다음 자리의 불확실성은 실제 거리로 보면 클 수 있다. → 일출 시각 예측에는 충분해도 위성 궤도 계산에는 더 높은 정확도가 필요하다.

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 우리말에 맞게 낱말을 모두 배열해 영어 문장을 쓰세요.
지구와 태양 사이의 거리, 즉 연중 한 지점에서 측정된 1.49597 × 10⁸km의 예를 들어 보자.

sun: / example, / as / the / between / km, / × / at / for / one / during / and / Earth / 1.49597 / distance / the / the / 10⁸ / measured / point / year / Take,
questions.a: Take, for example, the distance between Earth and the sun: 1.49597 × 10⁸ km, as measured at one point during the year
questions.e: 지구와 태양 사이의 거리, 즉 연중 한 지점에서 측정된 1.49597 × 10⁸km의 예를 들어 보자.

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 우리말에 맞게 낱말을 모두 배열해 영어 문장을 쓰세요.
따라서 인용된 숫자가 ‘정확한지’ 아닌지는 내가 그것으로 무엇을 하려고 하느냐에 따라 다르다.

the / do / to / on / I’m / therefore / not / with / is / intending / Whether / number / depends / what / it / quoted / or / “precise”
questions.a: Whether or not the quoted number is “precise” therefore depends on what I’m intending to do with it
questions.e: 따라서 인용된 숫자가 ‘정확한지’ 아닌지는 내가 그것으로 무엇을 하려고 하느냐에 따라 다르다.

questions.q:
[11-14 정확함은 쓰임새에 달려 있다] 우리말에 맞게 낱말을 모두 배열해 영어 문장을 쓰세요.
만약 내가 내일 태양이 몇 분에 뜰지에만 관심이 있다면 여기 인용된 숫자로 괜찮다.

what / number / care / is / fine / minute / rise / the / tomorrow, / I / only / sun / then / the / here / If / quoted / will / about
questions.a: If I care only about what minute the sun will rise tomorrow, then the number quoted here is fine
questions.e: 만약 내가 내일 태양이 몇 분에 뜰지에만 관심이 있다면 여기 인용된 숫자로 괜찮다.

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
At the Leipzig Zoo in Germany, 34 zoo chimpanzees and orangutans [ participating / participated ] in a study were each individually tested in a room, where they were put in front of two boxes.
questions.e: participating은 유인원이 연구에 참여하는 능동 관계를 나타낸다. 주어는 chimpanzees and orangutans이므로 주절 동사는 were이다.

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
An experimenter would place an object inside one box and [ leaving / leave ] the room.
questions.e: would 뒤에 place와 leave가 and로 병렬 연결되어 모두 동사원형을 쓴다.

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
Another experimenter would enter the room, [ move / moving ] the object into the other box and exit.
questions.e: enter, move, exit가 would를 공유한다. 물건을 옮긴 사람은 두 번째 실험자이다.

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
When the first experimenter returned and tried retrieving the object from the first box, the great ape would help the experimenter [ opening / open ] the second box, which it knew the object had been transferred to.
questions.e: 필기: help는 5형식으로 쓰여 목적어 뒤에 동사원형 또는 to부정사를 받는다. which절의 it은 유인원을 가리킨다.

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
However, most apes in the study did not help the first experimenter open the second box if the first experimenter was still in the room to see the second experimenter [ move / to move ] the item.
questions.e: 필기: see + 목적어 + 동사원형 move이며 moving도 가능하다. to move는 이 구조의 목적격 보어로 쓸 수 없다.

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
The findings [ shows / show ] the great apes understood when the first experimenter still thought the item was where he or she last left it.
questions.e: 필기에서 주제로 표시한 문장이다. findings는 복수이므로 show이며 뒤에는 목적어절의 that이 생략되어 있다.

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
According to the study, great apes can distinguish [ whether / that ] or not people have a(n) false belief about reality and use this understanding to help people.
questions.e: whether or not은 ‘~인지 아닌지’를 뜻한다. distinguish와 use가 can을 공유하며 본문 실험을 능력과 활용이라는 두 요소로 압축한다.

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
At the Leipzig Zoo in Germany, 34 zoo chimpanzees and orangutans participating in a study were each [ collectively / individually ] tested in a room, where they were put in front of two boxes.
questions.e: 각 유인원을 한 마리씩 따로 시험했다.

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
An experimenter would place an object inside one box and [ leave / remain in ] the room.
questions.e: 첫 번째 실험자가 방을 떠나야 물건 이동을 보지 못하는 조건이 성립한다.

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
Another experimenter would enter the room, move the object into [ the same box / the other box ] and exit.
questions.e: 두 상자 중 나머지 상자로 물건의 위치를 바꾼다.

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
When the first experimenter returned and tried retrieving the object from the first box, the great ape would help the experimenter open [ the second box / the first box ], which it knew the object had been transferred to.
questions.e: 유인원은 물건의 실제 위치를 모르는 실험자를 실제 위치로 이끈다.

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
However, most apes in the study [ always helped / did not help ] the first experimenter open the second box if the first experimenter was still in the room to see the second experimenter move the item.
questions.e: 실험자가 이동을 보아 위치를 아는 경우에는 같은 도움을 주지 않았다.

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
The findings show the great apes understood when the first experimenter [ still thought / already knew ] the item was where he or she last left it.
questions.e: 실험자의 믿음이 실제 위치와 어긋나는 상황을 유인원이 이해했다.

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
According to the study, great apes can distinguish whether or not people have a(n) [ accurate knowledge / false belief ] about reality and use this understanding to help people.
questions.e: 핵심은 다른 사람의 잘못된 믿음을 파악하고 그에 맞추어 돕는 능력이다.

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 다음 문장의 “individually”은(는) ‘개별적으로’(으)로 해석된다.
At the Leipzig Zoo in Germany, 34 zoo chimpanzees and orangutans participating in a study were each individually tested in a room, where they were put in front of two boxes.
questions.e: individually = 개별적으로

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 다음 문장의 “leave”은(는) ‘떠나곤’(으)로 해석된다.
An experimenter would place an object inside one box and leave the room.
questions.e: leave = 떠나곤

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 다음 문장의 “the other box”은(는) ‘다른 상자’(으)로 해석된다.
Another experimenter would enter the room, move the object into the other box and exit.
questions.e: the other box = 다른 상자

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 다음 문장의 “the second box”은(는) ‘재구성하면서’(으)로 해석된다.
When the first experimenter returned and tried retrieving the object from the first box, the great ape would help the experimenter open the second box, which it knew the object had been transferred to.
questions.e: the second box = 두 번째 상자

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 다음 문장의 “did not help”은(는) ‘궤도에서 벗어나게’(으)로 해석된다.
However, most apes in the study did not help the first experimenter open the second box if the first experimenter was still in the room to see the second experimenter move the item.
questions.e: did not help = 돕지 않았다

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 다음 문장의 “still thought”은(는) ‘사회적 비용’(으)로 해석된다.
The findings show the great apes understood when the first experimenter still thought the item was where he or she last left it.
questions.e: still thought = 여전히 생각하는

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 다음 문장의 “false belief”은(는) ‘선입견’(으)로 해석된다.
According to the study, great apes can distinguish whether or not people have a(n) false belief about reality and use this understanding to help people.
questions.e: false belief = 잘못된 믿음

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 순서로 알맞은 것은?
At the Leipzig Zoo in Germany, 34 zoo chimpanzees and orangutans participating in a study were each individually tested in a room, where they were put in front of two boxes.

(A) However, most apes in the study did not help the first experimenter open the second box if the first experimenter was still in the room to see the second experimenter move the item. The findings show the great apes understood when the first experimenter still thought the item was where he or she last left it.
(B) An experimenter would place an object inside one box and leave the room.
(C) Another experimenter would enter the room, move the object into the other box and exit. When the first experimenter returned and tried retrieving the object from the first box, the great ape would help the experimenter open the second box, which it knew the object had been transferred to.
questions.e: 두 상자 앞에서 침팬지·오랑우탄을 개별 실험함 → 첫 실험자가 없을 때 다른 사람이 물건을 옮김 → 옮긴 것을 모르는 실험자에게는 두 번째 상자를 열어 줌 → 이동을 본 실험자에게는 같은 도움을 주지 않음 · 마지막 요약문은 순서 배열에서 제외합니다.

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 본문을 요약한 문장의 빈칸에 알맞은 말은?
According to the study, great apes can distinguish whether or not people have a(n) [ accurate knowledge / false belief ] about reality and use this understanding to help people.
questions.e: 문장 4: 첫 실험자가 돌아와 첫 상자에서 물건을 꺼내려 했을 때, 유인원은 실험자가 두 번째 상자를 열도록 도왔는데, 유인원은 물건이 그곳으로 옮겨졌음을 알고 있었다. / 문장 5: 하지만 연구의 대부분의 유인원은 첫 실험자가 두 번째 상자를 열도록 돕지 않았다 첫 실험자가 방에 계속 있어서 두 번째 실험자가 물건을 옮기는 것을 본 경우에는. / 문장 6: 연구 결과는 유인원들이 첫 실험자가 물건이 마지막으로 둔 곳에 있다고 여전히 생각하는 상황을 이해했음을 보여 준다.

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 본문을 요약한 문장의 빈칸에 알맞은 말은?
According to the study, great apes can distinguish whether or not people have a(n) false belief about reality and use this understanding to [ help / mislead ] people.
questions.e: 문장 4: 첫 실험자가 돌아와 첫 상자에서 물건을 꺼내려 했을 때, 유인원은 실험자가 두 번째 상자를 열도록 도왔는데, 유인원은 물건이 그곳으로 옮겨졌음을 알고 있었다. / 문장 5: 하지만 연구의 대부분의 유인원은 첫 실험자가 두 번째 상자를 열도록 돕지 않았다 첫 실험자가 방에 계속 있어서 두 번째 실험자가 물건을 옮기는 것을 본 경우에는.

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 우리말에 맞게 낱말을 모두 배열해 영어 문장을 쓰세요.
한 실험자가 한 상자 안에 물건을 놓고 방을 떠나곤 했다.

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 우리말에 맞게 낱말을 모두 배열해 영어 문장을 쓰세요.

questions.q:
[15-15 유인원은 남의 착각을 알아챌까] 우리말에 맞게 낱말을 모두 배열해 영어 문장을 쓰세요.

and / use / study, / to / not / apes / can / understanding / great / this / to / distinguish / or / people / false / a(n) / reality / belief / people / have / According / about / whether / help / the
questions.a: According to the study, great apes can distinguish whether or not people have a(n) false belief about reality and use this understanding to help people
questions.e: 이 연구에 따르면 유인원은 사람이 현실에 대해 잘못된 믿음을 갖는지 구별하고 이러한 이해를 사람을 돕는 데 사용할 수 있다.

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
One way that music could express emotion [ is / are ] simply through a learned association.
questions.e: 필기: 주어의 핵은 단수 One way이다. that music could express emotion은 way를 수식하므로 동사는 is이다.

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
Perhaps there is nothing naturally sad about a piece of music in a minor key, or [ playing / played ] slowly with low notes.
questions.e: 악곡은 연주되는 대상이므로 played를 쓴다. nothing naturally sad에서는 형용사 sad가 nothing을 뒤에서 수식한다.

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
Maybe we have just come to hear certain kinds of music as sad because we have learned [ to associate / associating ] them in our culture with sad events like funerals.
questions.e: learn to associate는 ‘연관시키는 것을 배우다’이며 associate them with sad events에서 them은 음악을 받는다.

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
If this view is correct, we should have difficulty [ to interpret / interpreting ] the emotions expressed in culturally unfamiliar music.
questions.e: 필기: difficulty 뒤의 in은 생략 가능하며 interpreting은 동명사이다. expressed는 감정이 표현된 수동 관계이다.

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
Totally [ opposed / opposing ] to this view is the position that the link between music and emotion is one of resemblance.
questions.e: 필기: C+V+S 순서이다. 원래 주어는 the position이고 Totally opposed to this view가 앞으로 나온 보어이다. that절은 position의 내용이다.

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
For example, when we feel sad we move [ slow / slowly ] and speak slowly and in a low-pitched voice.
questions.e: move와 speak를 수식하므로 slowly이다. low-pitched는 명사 voice를 수식하는 형용사이다.

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
Thus when we hear slow, low music, we hear it as [ sad / sadly ].
questions.e: hear it as sad는 ‘그 음악을 슬픈 것으로 듣다’이다. sad는 음악의 성격을 나타내고 hear의 방식을 나타내는 sadly와 다르다.

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
If this view is correct, we should have little difficulty [ to understand / understanding ] the emotion expressed in culturally unfamiliar music.
questions.e: 필기: understanding은 동명사이다. little difficulty는 ‘어려움이 거의 없음’이므로 앞 관점의 예측과 반대이다.

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
It is believed that emotion expressed in music can be [ understood / understanding ] through a culturally learned association or it can be understood due to the similarity between music and emotion.
questions.e: 감정은 이해되는 대상이므로 can be understood이다. 요약문은 or로 서로 다른 두 설명을 나란히 압축한다.

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
One way that music could express emotion is simply through a [ innate identity / learned association ].
questions.e: 첫 입장은 음악의 감정 의미를 문화적으로 학습한 연결로 설명한다.

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
Perhaps there is nothing [ naturally sad / necessarily cheerful ] about a piece of music in a minor key, or played slowly with low notes.
questions.e: 이 입장에서는 느리고 낮은 음악 자체에 타고난 슬픔이 있는 것은 아니라고 본다.

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
Maybe we have just come to hear certain kinds of music as sad because we have learned to associate them in our culture with sad events like [ celebrations / funerals ].
questions.e: 문화적으로 슬픔과 연결되는 행사에 음악이 쓰인 경험이 연관을 만든다.

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
If this view is correct, we should have [ difficulty / no trouble ] interpreting the emotions expressed in culturally unfamiliar music.
questions.e: 학습된 연관이 필요하다면 문화 경험이 없는 음악은 해석하기 어렵다.

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
Totally opposed to this view is the position that the link between music and emotion is one of [ cultural convention / resemblance ].
questions.e: 두 번째 입장은 학습보다 음악과 감정 사이의 닮음을 강조한다.

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
For example, when we feel sad we move slowly and speak slowly and in a [ low-pitched voice / high-pitched voice ].
questions.e: 슬플 때의 목소리와 음악의 낮은 음이 닮았다는 근거이다.

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
Thus when we hear [ fast, high music / slow, low music ], we hear it as sad.
questions.e: 슬픔의 행동적 특징과 닮은 음악을 슬픈 것으로 듣는다는 설명이다.

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
If this view is correct, we should have [ little difficulty / great difficulty ] understanding the emotion expressed in culturally unfamiliar music.
questions.e: 유사성이 핵심이라면 문화가 달라도 음악의 감정을 이해하기 쉽다.

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
It is believed that emotion expressed in music can be understood through a culturally learned association or it can be understood due to the [ unrelatedness / similarity ] between music and emotion.
questions.e: 요약문은 학습된 연관과 유사성이라는 두 관점을 모두 포함해야 한다.

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 다음 문장의 “learned association”은(는) ‘빠르게’(으)로 해석된다.
One way that music could express emotion is simply through a learned association.
questions.e: learned association = 학습된 연관

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 다음 문장의 “naturally sad”은(는) ‘확실한 손실’(으)로 해석된다.
Perhaps there is nothing naturally sad about a piece of music in a minor key, or played slowly with low notes.
questions.e: naturally sad = 본질적으로 슬픈

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 다음 문장의 “funerals”은(는) ‘거미’(으)로 해석된다.
Maybe we have just come to hear certain kinds of music as sad because we have learned to associate them in our culture with sad events like funerals.
questions.e: funerals = 장례식

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 다음 문장의 “difficulty”은(는) ‘어려움’(으)로 해석된다.
If this view is correct, we should have difficulty interpreting the emotions expressed in culturally unfamiliar music.
questions.e: difficulty = 어려움

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 다음 문장의 “resemblance”은(는) ‘유사성’(으)로 해석된다.
Totally opposed to this view is the position that the link between music and emotion is one of resemblance.
questions.e: resemblance = 유사성

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 다음 문장의 “low-pitched voice”은(는) ‘낮은 목소리’(으)로 해석된다.
For example, when we feel sad we move slowly and speak slowly and in a low-pitched voice.
questions.e: low-pitched voice = 낮은 목소리

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 다음 문장의 “slow, low music”은(는) ‘느리고 낮은 음의 음악’(으)로 해석된다.
Thus when we hear slow, low music, we hear it as sad.
questions.e: slow, low music = 느리고 낮은 음의 음악

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 다음 문장의 “little difficulty”은(는) ‘어려움이 거의 없을’(으)로 해석된다.
If this view is correct, we should have little difficulty understanding the emotion expressed in culturally unfamiliar music.
questions.e: little difficulty = 어려움이 거의 없을

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 다음 문장의 “similarity”은(는) ‘유사성’(으)로 해석된다.
It is believed that emotion expressed in music can be understood through a culturally learned association or it can be understood due to the similarity between music and emotion.
questions.e: similarity = 유사성

questions.q:
[15-16 음악은 어떻게 슬픔을 전할까] 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 순서로 알맞은 것은?
One way that music could express emotion is simply through a learned association.

(A) For example, when we feel sad we move slowly and speak slowly and in a low-pitched voice. Thus when we hear slow, low music, we hear it as sad. If this view is correct, we should have little difficulty understanding the emotion expressed in culturally unfamiliar music.
(B) Perhaps there is nothing naturally sad about a piece of music in a minor key, or played slowly with low notes. Maybe we have just come to hear certain kinds of music as sad because we have learned to associate them in our culture with sad events like funerals.
(C) If this view is correct, we should have difficulty interpreting the emotions expressed in culturally unfamiliar music. Totally opposed to this view is the position that the link between music and emotion is one of resemblance.

questions.q:

questions.e: in captivity는 이 문장에서 갇힌 상태에서의 의미로 쓰인다.

Capuchins — New World Monkeys that live in large social groups — will, in captivity, trade with people all day long, especially if food is involved.

(A) Even though she is still getting “paid” the same amount for her effort of sourcing rocks, and so her particular situation has not changed, the comparison to another makes the situation unfair. Furthermore, she is now willing to abandon all gains — the cucumbers themselves — to communicate her displeasure to the experimenter.

(C) If you put two monkeys in cages next to each other, and offer them both slices of cucumber for the rocks they already have, they will happily eat the cucumbers. If, however, you give one monkey grapes instead — grapes being universally preferred to cucumbers — the monkey that is still receiving cucumbers will begin to throw them back at the experimenter.

questions.e: less complicated = 덜 복잡한

questions.q:
[15-23 미디어가 과학을 단순화하는 이유] 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 순서로 알맞은 것은?
There is often a lot of uncertainty in the realm of science, which the general public finds uncomfortable.

(A) A perfect example of this is how people want definitive answers as to which foods are “good” and “bad.” Scientifically speaking, there are no “good” and “bad” foods; rather, food quality exists on a continuum meaning that some foods are better than others when it comes to general health and well-being.
(B) They don’t want “informed guesses,” they want certainties that make their lives easier, and science is often unequipped to meet these demands. In particular, the human body is fantastically complex, and some scientific answers can never be provided in black-or-white terms.
(C) All this is why the media tends to oversimplify scientific research when presenting it to the public. In their eyes, they’re just “giving people what they want” as opposed to offering more accurate but complex information that very few people will read or understand.
questions.e: 대중은 불확실성을 불편해하고 확실한 답을 원함 → 인체 등 복잡한 문제에는 흑백 답이 불가능함 → 미디어는 복잡한 정확성보다 대중이 원하는 단순함을 제공함 → 음식의 질도 좋음·나쁨의 이분법이 아니라 연속체임 · 마지막 요약문은 순서 배열에서 제외합니다.

questions.q:

questions.e: 필기: 강조 대상은 목적어이며 원래 문장은 Consumers find the uncertainty ... attractive이다.

questions.e: on은 전치사이므로 developing을 쓴다. 필기: core product는 스포츠 경기 그 자체이다.

questions.q:
[15-31 예측할 수 없는 스포츠의 마케팅] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.

questions.q:

This [ heterogeneity / uniformity ] is a feature of sport.
questions.e: heterogeneity는 이 문장에서 이질성의 의미로 쓰인다.

questions.q:
[15-31 예측할 수 없는 스포츠의 마케팅] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
It is the [ complete predictability / uncertainty ] of the result and the quality of the contest that consumers find attractive.
questions.e: uncertainty는 이 문장에서 불확실성의 의미로 쓰인다.

questions.q:
[15-31 예측할 수 없는 스포츠의 마케팅] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
For the sport marketer, this is [ problematic / fully controllable ], as the quality of the contest cannot be guaranteed, no promises can be made in relations to the result and no assurances can be given in respect of the performance of star players.
questions.e: problematic는 이 문장에서 문제가 된다의 의미로 쓰인다.

questions.q:
[15-31 예측할 수 없는 스포츠의 마케팅] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
Unlike consumer products, sport cannot and does not display [ constant variation / consistency ] as a key feature of marketing strategies.
questions.e: consistency는 이 문장에서 일관성의 의미로 쓰인다.

questions.q:
[15-31 예측할 수 없는 스포츠의 마케팅] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
The sport marketer therefore must avoid marketing strategies based solely on winning, and must instead focus on developing [ product extensions / winning alone ] such as the facility, parking, merchandise, souvenirs, food and beverages rather than on the core product (that is, the game itself).
questions.e: product extensions는 이 문장에서 제품 확장의 의미로 쓰인다.

questions.q:
[15-31 예측할 수 없는 스포츠의 마케팅] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
Sport has the essential nature of being unreliable, which requires that its marketing strategies feature [ only the final score / products and services ] more than just the sports match.
questions.e: products and services는 이 문장에서 상품과 서비스의 의미로 쓰인다.

It is the uncertainty of the result and the quality of the contest that consumers find attractive.
questions.e: uncertainty = 불확실성

questions.q:
[15-31 예측할 수 없는 스포츠의 마케팅] 다음 문장의 “problematic”은(는) ‘문제가 된다’(으)로 해석된다.
For the sport marketer, this is problematic, as the quality of the contest cannot be guaranteed, no promises can be made in relations to the result and no assurances can be given in respect of the performance of star players.
questions.e: problematic = 문제가 된다

[15-31 예측할 수 없는 스포츠의 마케팅] 다음 문장의 “consistency”은(는) ‘덜 복잡한’(으)로 해석된다.
Unlike consumer products, sport cannot and does not display consistency as a key feature of marketing strategies.

[15-31 예측할 수 없는 스포츠의 마케팅] 다음 문장의 “product extensions”은(는) ‘차이’(으)로 해석된다.
The sport marketer therefore must avoid marketing strategies based solely on winning, and must instead focus on developing product extensions such as the facility, parking, merchandise, souvenirs, food and beverages rather than on the core product (that is, the game itself).

questions.q:
[15-31 예측할 수 없는 스포츠의 마케팅] 다음 문장의 “products and services”은(는) ‘상품과 서비스’(으)로 해석된다.
Sport has the essential nature of being unreliable, which requires that its marketing strategies feature products and services more than just the sports match.
questions.e: products and services = 상품과 서비스

[15-31 예측할 수 없는 스포츠의 마케팅] 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 순서로 알맞은 것은?

questions.q:

questions.e: 문장 6: 따라서 스포츠 마케터는 승리에만 기초한 전략을 피하고 핵심 제품인 경기 자체보다 시설, 주차, 상품, 기념품, 식음료 같은 제품 확장 개발에 집중해야 한다.

[15-31 예측할 수 없는 스포츠의 마케팅] 우리말에 맞게 낱말을 모두 배열해 영어 문장을 쓰세요.
이러한 이질성은 스포츠의 특징이다.

is / a / heterogeneity / of / feature / This / sport
questions.a: This heterogeneity is a feature of sport
questions.e: 이러한 이질성은 스포츠의 특징이다.

[15-31 예측할 수 없는 스포츠의 마케팅] 우리말에 맞게 낱말을 모두 배열해 영어 문장을 쓰세요.

has / services / nature / marketing / the / being / which / feature / its / requires / strategies / the / sports / essential / more / match / that / and / than / just / Sport / unreliable, / products / of

questions.e: 스포츠는 불확실하다는 본질적 속성이 있고 이는 마케팅 전략이 스포츠 경기만이 아니라 상품과 서비스를 특징으로 삼도록 요구한다.

questions.q:
[15-32 오히려 행동을 부추기는 트릭 처벌] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
Punishing a child may not be effective due to [ what / that ] Álvaro Bilbao, a neuropsychologist, calls “trick-punishments.”
questions.e: 필기: due to는 전치사 표현이며 what은 calls의 목적어를 겸하여 ‘~라고 부르는 것’을 뜻한다.

questions.q:
[15-32 오히려 행동을 부추기는 트릭 처벌] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
A trick-punishment is a scolding, a moment of anger or a punishment in the most [ classically / classic ] sense of the word.
questions.e: sense를 수식하므로 classic이라는 형용사를 쓴다.

questions.q:
[15-32 오히려 행동을 부추기는 트릭 처벌] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.
Instead of discouraging the child from [ doing / to do ] something, it encourages them to do it.
questions.e: 필기: from은 전치사이므로 doing이다. encourages them to do에서는 to부정사가 목적격 보어이다.

questions.q:
[15-32 오히려 행동을 부추기는 트릭 처벌] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.

questions.e: that절의 주어 his mother는 단수이므로 scolds이다.

questions.q:

questions.q:

questions.q:

questions.q:
[15-32 오히려 행동을 부추기는 트릭 처벌] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.

questions.q:
[15-32 오히려 행동을 부추기는 트릭 처벌] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.

questions.e: can 뒤에는 동사원형 avoid이다. This way는 긍정 행동을 보상하는 방식을 가리킨다.

questions.q:

questions.e: 전치사 on 뒤 reducing을 쓴다. while rewarding은 부모의 동시에 하는 행동을 나타낸다.

questions.q:

questions.e: not be effective는 이 문장에서 효과적이지 않을의 의미로 쓰인다.

questions.q:
[15-32 오히려 행동을 부추기는 트릭 처벌] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.
A trick-punishment is a [ scolding / silent approval ], a moment of anger or a punishment in the most classic sense of the word.
questions.e: scolding는 이 문장에서 꾸중의 의미로 쓰인다.

questions.q:

U.K. researchers say a bedtime of between 10 p.m. and 11 p.m. is best. They say people who go to sleep between these times have a lower risk of heart disease. Six years ago, the researchers collected data on the sleep patterns of 80,000 volunteers. The volunteers had to wear a special watch for seven days so the researchers could collect data on their sleeping and waking times. The scientists then monitored the health of the volunteers. Around 3,000 volunteers later showed heart problems. They went to bed earlier or later than the ideal 10 p.m. to 11 p.m. timeframe. One of the authors of the study, Dr. David Plans, commented on his research and the effects of bedtimes on the health of our heart. He said the study could not give a certain cause for their results, but it suggests that early or late bedtimes may be more likely to disrupt the body clock, with negative consequences for cardiovascular health. He said that it was important for our body to wake up to the morning light, and that the worst time to go to bed was after midnight because it may reduce the likelihood of seeing morning light which resets the body clock. He added that we risk cardiovascular disease if our body clock is not reset properly.

U.K. researchers say a bedtime of between 10 p.m. and 11 p.m. is best.

(A) One of the authors of the study, Dr. David Plans, commented on his research and the effects of bedtimes on the health of our heart. He said the study could not give a certain cause for their results, but it suggests that early or late bedtimes may be more likely to disrupt the body clock, with negative consequences for cardiovascular health. He said that it was important for our body to wake up to the morning light, and that the worst time to go to bed was after midnight because it may reduce the likelihood of seeing morning light which resets the body clock. He added that we risk cardiovascular disease if our body clock is not reset properly.
(B) They say people who go to sleep between these times have a lower risk of heart disease. Six years ago, the researchers collected data on the sleep patterns of 80,000 volunteers. The volunteers had to wear a special watch for seven days so the researchers could collect data on their sleeping and waking times.
(C) The scientists then monitored the health of the volunteers. Around 3,000 volunteers later showed heart problems. They went to bed earlier or later than the ideal 10 p.m. to 11 p.m. timeframe.

But when we try something new in our adult lives we’ll usually make just one attempt before judging whether it’s worked. Mike May lost his sight at the age of three. Because he had spent the majority of his life adapting to being blind — and even cultivating a skiing career in this state — his other senses compensated by growing stronger. However, when his sight was restored through a surgery in his forties, his entire perception of reality was disrupted. Instead of being thrilled that he could see now, as he’d expected, his brain was so overloaded with new visual stimuli that the world became a frightening and overwhelming place. After he’d learned to know his family through touch and smell, he found that he couldn’t recognize his children with his eyes, and this left him puzzled. Skiing also became a lot harder as he struggled to adapt to the visual stimulation. This confusion occurred because his brain hadn’t yet learned to see. Though we often tend to assume our eyes function as video cameras which relay information to our brain, advances in neuroscientific research have proven that this is actually not the case. Instead, sight is a collaborative effort between our eyes and our brains, and the way we process visual reality depends on the way these two communicate. If communication between our eyes and our brains is disturbed, our perception of reality is altered accordingly. And because other areas of May’s brain had adapted to process information primarily through his other senses, the process of learning how to see was more difficult than he’d anticipated.

questions.e: 시각은 눈이 영상을 전달하는 것만으로 완성되지 않는다. 눈과 뇌가 협력하며 뇌도 시각 정보를 해석하는 법을 배워야 한다.

Mike May lost his sight at the age of three.

(A) Though we often tend to assume our eyes function as video cameras which relay information to our brain, advances in neuroscientific research have proven that this is actually not the case. Instead, sight is a collaborative effort between our eyes and our brains, and the way we process visual reality depends on the way these two communicate. If communication between our eyes and our brains is disturbed, our perception of reality is altered accordingly. And because other areas of May’s brain had adapted to process information primarily through his other senses, the process of learning how to see was more difficult than he’d anticipated.
(B) Because he had spent the majority of his life adapting to being blind — and even cultivating a skiing career in this state — his other senses compensated by growing stronger. However, when his sight was restored through a surgery in his forties, his entire perception of reality was disrupted. Instead of being thrilled that he could see now, as he’d expected, his brain was so overloaded with new visual stimuli that the world became a frightening and overwhelming place.
(C) After he’d learned to know his family through touch and smell, he found that he couldn’t recognize his children with his eyes, and this left him puzzled. Skiing also became a lot harder as he struggled to adapt to the visual stimulation. This confusion occurred because his brain hadn’t yet learned to see.

questions.q:

Most of these leaders had to hunt and gather along with the other members because the surpluses of food and other vital resources were seldom sufficient to support a full-time chief or village council. In return, the nonfarmers provided leadership and security for the farming population, enabling it to continue to increase food/energy yields and provide ever larger surpluses. With improved technology and favorable conditions, agriculture produced consistent surpluses of the basic necessities, and population groups grew in size. These groups concentrated in towns and cities, and human tasks specialized further. Specialists such as carpenters, blacksmiths, merchants, traders, and sailors developed their skills and became more efficient in their use of time and energy. The goods and services they provided brought about an improved quality of life, a higher standard of living and, for most societies, increased stability.

(A) With improved technology and favorable conditions, agriculture produced consistent surpluses of the basic necessities, and population groups grew in size. These groups concentrated in towns and cities, and human tasks specialized further. Specialists such as carpenters, blacksmiths, merchants, traders, and sailors developed their skills and became more efficient in their use of time and energy. The goods and services they provided brought about an improved quality of life, a higher standard of living and, for most societies, increased stability.
(B) A chief or group of elders usually led the camp or village. The development of agriculture changed work patterns.
(C) Early farmers could reap 3–10 kg of grain from each 1 kg of seed planted. Since the turn of the twentieth century we’ve believed in genetic causes of diagnoses — a theory called genetic determinism. Under this model, our genes and subsequent health are determined at birth. We are “destined” to inherit certain diseases based on the misfortune of our DNA. Genetic determinism doesn’t consider the role of family backgrounds, traumas, habits, or anything else within the environment. In this dynamic we are not active participants in our own health and wellness. Why would we be? If something is predetermined, it’s not necessary to look at anything beyond our DNA. But the more science has learned about the body and its interaction with the environment around it in its various forms, from our nutrition to our relationships to our racially oppressive systems, the more complicated the story becomes. We are not merely expressions of coding but products of a remarkable variety of interactions that are both within and outside of our control. Once we see beyond the narrative that genetics are destiny, we can take ownership of our health. This allows us to see how “choiceless” we once were and empowers us with the ability to create real and lasting change.

The longest journey we will make is the eighteen inches between our head and heart.

(A) Cut someone off in traffic? Splashed someone in a pool? Or made a negative statement about something we’ve read? It helps to remember that a piece of us resides in every person we meet.
(B) If we take this journey, it can shorten our misery in the world. Impatience, judgment, frustration, and anger reside in our heads. When we live in that place too long, it makes us unhappy. But when we take the journey from our heads to our hearts, something shifts inside.
(C) What if we were able to love everything that gets in our way? What if we tried loving the shopper who unknowingly steps in front of us in line, the driver who cuts us off in traffic, the swimmer who splashes us with water during a belly dive, or the reader who pens a bad online review of our writing? Every person who makes us miserable is like us — a human being, most likely doing the best they can, deeply loved by their parents, a child, or a friend. Norms are everywhere, defining what is “normal” and guiding our interpretations of social life at every turn.

(A) Not knowing the norms of another community is the central problem of cross-cultural communication. To continue the Thank you example, even though another culture may have an expression that appears translatable (many don’t), there may be different norms for its usage, for example, such that you should say Thank you only when the cost someone has caused is considerable. In such a case it would sound ridiculous (i.e., unexpected, surprising, and worthy of criticism) if you were to thank someone for something so minor as holding a door open for you.

(A) The progression from one step to the next may not be clear, creating unavoidable large increases in difficulty from one to the next. People around you aren’t robots that you can endlessly experiment with for your own purposes. This is not to say that facing your fears is pointless when socializing. The principles of gradual exposure are still very useful. The process of applying them is just messier, and knowing that before you start is helpful.

Claims that local food production cut greenhouse gas emissions by reducing the burning of transportation fuel are usually not well founded.

(A) When food does travel, what matters most is not the distance traveled but the travel mode (surface versus air), and most of all the load size. Bulk loads of food can travel halfway around the world by ocean freight with a smaller carbon footprint, per pound delivered, than foods traveling just a short distance but in much smaller loads. For example, 18-wheelers carry much larger loads than pickup trucks so they can move food 100 times as far while burning only one-third as much gas per pound of food delivered.
(B) Transport is the source of only 11 percent of greenhouse gas emissions within the food sector, so reducing the distance that food travels after it leaves the farm is far less important than reducing wasteful energy use on the farm. Food coming from a distance can actually be better for the climate, depending on how it was grown.
(C) For example, field-grown tomatoes shipped from Mexico in the winter months will have a smaller carbon footprint than local winter tomatoes grown in a greenhouse. In the United Kingdom, lamb meat that travels 11,000 miles from New Zealand generates only one-quarter the carbon emissions per pound compared to British lamb because farmers in the United Kingdom raise their animals on feed which must be produced using fossil fuels rather than on clover pastureland.

questions.e: 필기: food available은 이용 가능한 음식이라는 후치 수식이다. Even though는 일부 지역과 전체 경향의 양보 관계이다.

questions.q:
[16-54 과식은 몸에 새겨진 생존 습관] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.

questions.q:

questions.q:
[16-54 과식은 몸에 새겨진 생존 습관] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.

[16-54 과식은 몸에 새겨진 생존 습관] 문맥상 알맞은 낱말을 고르세요.

questions.q:
[16-54 과식은 몸에 새겨진 생존 습관] 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 알맞은 것은?
A quick look at history shows that humans have not always had the abundance of food that is enjoyed throughout most of the developed world today. In fact, there have been numerous times in history when food has been rather scarce. As a result, people used to eat more when food was available since the availability of the next meal was questionable. Overeating in those times was essential to ensure survival, and humans received satisfaction from eating more than was needed for immediate purposes. On top of that, the highest pleasure was derived from eating the most calorie-dense foods, resulting in a longer lasting energy reserve. Even though there are parts of the world where, unfortunately, food is still scarce, most of the world’s population today has plenty of food available to survive and thrive. However, this abundance is new, and your body has not caught up, still naturally rewarding you for eating more than you need and for eating the most calorie-dense foods. These are innate habits and not simple addictions. They are self-preserving mechanisms initiated by your body, ensuring your future survival, but they are irrelevant now. Therefore, it is your responsibility to communicate with your body regarding the new environment of food abundance and the need to change the inborn habit of overeating.
c: 식량이 풍부해지면 과식 본능은 자동으로 사라진다
고열량 음식이 언제나 건강한 선택인 이유

Overeating in those times was essential to ensure survival, and humans received satisfaction from eating more than was needed for immediate purposes.
(C) On top of that, the highest pleasure was derived from eating the most calorie-dense foods, resulting in a longer lasting energy reserve. Even though there are parts of the world where, unfortunately, food is still scarce, most of the world’s population today has plenty of food available to survive and thrive. However, this abundance is new, and your body has not caught up, still naturally rewarding you for eating more than you need and for eating the most calorie-dense foods.

questions.q:

questions.e: 필기: what sort of thing 뒤에는 주어 it과 동사 is의 평서문 어순이 온다.

questions.q:

questions.q:

questions.q:
[16-55 사물에도 의도를 부여하는 이유] 어법상 알맞은 것을 고르세요.

questions.q:

questions.q:
[16-55 사물에도 의도를 부여하는 이유] 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 알맞은 것은?
From an early age, we assign purpose to objects and events, preferring this reasoning to random chance. Children assume, for instance, that pointy rocks are that way because they don’t want you to sit on them. When we encounter something, we first need to determine what sort of thing it is. Inanimate objects and plants generally do not move and can be evaluated from physics alone. However, by attributing intention to animals and even objects, we are able to make fast decisions about the likely behaviour of that being. This was essential in our hunter-gatherer days to avoid being eaten by predators. The anthropologist Stewart Guthrie made the point that survival in our evolutionary past meant that we interpret ambiguous objects as agents with human mental characteristics, as those are the mental processes which we understand. Ambiguous events are caused by such agents. This results in a perceptual system strongly biased towards anthropomorphism. Therefore, we tend to assume intention even where there is none. This would have arisen as a survival mechanism. If a lion is about to attack you, you need to react quickly, given its probable intention to kill you. By the time you have realized that the design of its teeth and claws could kill you, you are dead. So, assuming intent, without detailed design analysis or understanding of the physics, has saved your life.
c: 물리적 구조를 끝까지 분석해야만 생존할 수 있다
날카로운 돌의 모양이 생기는 지질 과정
questions.e: 인간이 모호한 사물이나 사건에 의도를 가정하는 의인화 편향은 포식자의 행동을 빠르게 판단해 생존하도록 돕던 기제에서 나왔다.

questions.q:

From an early age, we assign purpose to objects and events, preferring this reasoning to random chance.

(A) Therefore, we tend to assume intention even where there is none. This would have arisen as a survival mechanism. If a lion is about to attack you, you need to react quickly, given its probable intention to kill you. By the time you have realized that the design of its teeth and claws could kill you, you are dead. So, assuming intent, without detailed design analysis or understanding of the physics, has saved your life.
(B) Children assume, for instance, that pointy rocks are that way because they don’t want you to sit on them. When we encounter something, we first need to determine what sort of thing it is. Inanimate objects and plants generally do not move and can be evaluated from physics alone. However, by attributing intention to animals and even objects, we are able to make fast decisions about the likely behaviour of that being.
(C) This was essential in our hunter-gatherer days to avoid being eaten by predators. The anthropologist Stewart Guthrie made the point that survival in our evolutionary past meant that we interpret ambiguous objects as agents with human mental characteristics, as those are the mental processes which we understand. Ambiguous events are caused by such agents. This results in a perceptual system strongly biased towards anthropomorphism.

“May I help you?” are the worst four words that a retail salesperson can utter because they don’t encourage the customer to talk and put them on the defensive.

(A) The subconscious thought by the customer is often “I’m smart enough to figure out what I want, and I don’t need your help!” If customers feel pressured or cornered, then salespeople won’t make any sales. The approach has to promote a comfortable environment that makes customers feel there is no rush. Furthermore, if customers just want to look around, they should feel that it is all right to do so. In situations where customers really do want to look around on their own, salespeople should give customers their business cards and keep themselves accessible in case customers have questions or concerns.

Examples of better questions to use when approaching customers are “Is there anything in particular that you are looking for?” and “Are you shopping for a gift?” If a fashion salesperson approached you with “May I help you?” chances are you would feel the salesperson didn’t care. This almost always puts the customer on the defense. “No, thank you” is usually the immediate response, even if the customer is actually in need of assistance.
